name: Bṛhadīśvara temple, Thanjavur
summary: Granite Śiva temple built by the Cōḻa king Rājarāja I at his capital Thanjavur and consecrated in 1010 CE; its c. 60 m vimāna was the tallest of its age and the walls carry a large corpus of Rājarāja’s own Tamil inscriptions.
details:
The temple, called Rājarājeśvaram in its inscriptions, was built between c. 1003 and 1010 CE. Its inscriptions record that on the 275th day of Rājarāja I’s 25th regnal year (1010 CE) the king presented the gold-plated finial (kalaśa) for the vimāna, and they list endowments, temple staff and the bronzes the king and his family gave.

The circumambulatory passage around the sanctum preserves Cōḻa-period wall paintings (partly over-painted in the Nāyaka period). Later Nāyaka and Marāṭhā rulers of Thanjavur added subsidiary shrines and halls within the enclosure. The temple remains in worship.

name: Bṛhadīśvara temple, Gangaikondacholapuram
summary: Śiva temple at the new capital founded by Rājendra I after his northern campaign to the Gaṅgā (c. 1025); its vimāna has a gently concave profile, unlike Thanjavur’s straight-sided pyramid. Part of the Great Living Chola Temples World Heritage property.
details: Rājendra I (r. 1014–1044) took the title Gaṅgaikoṇḍa (“who took the Gaṅgā”) after his army reached the Gaṅgā and established the city of Gaṅgaikoṇḍacōḻapuram as Cōḻa capital around 1025; it remained the capital for about two and a half centuries. The temple is usually dated to c. 1035, i.e. within his reign. Famous sculptures include Śiva garlanding the devotee Caṇḍeśa.

dates.label: c. 1025–1044 CE (often given as c. 1035)
dates.basis: regnal synchronism with Rājendra I and his founding of the capital

name: Airāvateśvara temple, Darasuram
summary: Twelfth-century Śiva temple near Kumbakonam built under the Cōḻa king Rājarāja II; its maṇḍapa is designed as a stone chariot and its reliefs include narrative friezes of the 63 Nāyaṉmār saints.
details: The temple takes its name from the tradition that Indra’s white elephant Airāvata worshipped Śiva here. It is attributed to Rājarāja II (r. c. 1146–1173). Small labelled panels illustrate episodes from the lives of the Śaiva saints later collected in the Periya Purāṇam.

dates.basis: temple tradition (sthala-purāṇa / local narrative); not a historical date

limits: Dates the surviving fabric to the reign of Rājarāja II; the Airāvata legend is the temple’s own tradition and is not a historical date.

name: Naṭarāja temple, Chidambaram
summary: Temple of Śiva as Naṭarāja, the cosmic dancer, worshipped in the gold-roofed Kaṉakasabhā; it is the “ether” (ākāśa) shrine among the five element liṅgas and one of the most celebrated temples sung in the Tēvāram.
details:
Copper-plate inscriptions credit the Cōḻa king Parāntaka I (10th c.) with gilding the roof of the hall in which Naṭarāja dances. Most of the surviving plan and the great gopuras date from the late 12th and 13th centuries, with later additions. The temple is administered by the hereditary Dīkṣitar priests, and its ritual combines Vedic and Āgamic elements.

The temple tradition identifies Chidambaram as the place where Śiva performed the ānanda-tāṇḍava before the sages Patañjali and Vyāghrapāda; the “Chidambara rahasya” is worshipped as the formless ākāśa.

dates.label: Śiva danced the ānanda-tāṇḍava here before Patañjali and Vyāghrapāda (sthala tradition)

name: Śrī Raṅganāthasvāmī temple, Srirangam
summary: Island temple of Viṣṇu as Raṅganātha reclining on the serpent, set within seven concentric enclosures on an island of the Kāvēri; first among the 108 Divya Deśams of the Śrīvaiṣṇava tradition.
details:
The temple is praised in the hymns of the Āḻvārs collected in the Nālāyira Divya Prabandham. Its many inscriptions, from the Cōḻa period onwards, record gifts from Cōḻa, Pāṇḍya, Hoysaḷa and Vijayanagara rulers and show the temple’s role as a landholder and charitable institution. Rāmānuja is held by tradition to have spent his last decades here and organised its worship.

The outer Rājagopuram, about 73 m high, was completed only in 1987 with support from the Ahobila Maṭha.

dates.label: Image brought by Vibhīṣaṇa from Ayodhyā and left on the island (temple tradition)
dates.basis: temple tradition (sthala-purāṇa / local narrative); not a historical date

dates.basis: inscriptions from the Cōḻa period onward and architectural style

limits: Inscriptions and fabric document a temple continuously endowed from the Cōḻa period to modern times; the tradition that Vibhīṣaṇa left the image here is a sthala narrative, not evidence for the date of the cult.

name: Mīnākṣī–Sundareśvara temple, Madurai
summary: Twin-shrine temple of the goddess Mīnākṣī and her consort Sundareśvara (Śiva) at the heart of Madurai; its fourteen painted gopuras, the tallest c. 52 m, largely date from Nāyaka rebuilding in the 16th–17th centuries.
details: Madurai (Ālavāy) is celebrated in the Tēvāram, and the temple’s sacred history is told in the Tiruviḷaiyāṭaṟpurāṇam (the “sacred games” of Śiva). After the raids of the Delhi Sultanate armies in the early 14th century the temple was restored, and it was massively expanded by the Madurai Nāyakas in the 16th–17th centuries. The annual Cittirai festival re-enacts the marriage of Mīnākṣī and Sundareśvara, with Viṣṇu (Aḻakar) arriving as the bride’s brother.

dates.label: Mīnākṣī, born as a Pāṇḍya princess, married Śiva as Sundareśvara at Madurai (Tiruviḷaiyāṭaṟpurāṇam tradition)
dates.basis: temple tradition (sthala-purāṇa / local narrative); not a historical date

dates.label: 14th c. CE restoration after Sultanate-period destruction

limits: The surviving complex is predominantly Nāyaka-period; earlier phases are known from texts and inscriptions rather than standing fabric. The divine-marriage narrative is temple mythology and festival practice, not a historical event.

name: Rāmanāthasvāmī temple, Rameswaram
summary: Śiva temple on Pamban (Rameswaram) island where, according to tradition, Rāma worshipped a liṅga; it is counted among the twelve jyotirliṅgas and as the southern dhāma of the Char Dham, and is known for its very long pillared corridors.
details:
The temple tradition holds that Rāma, returning from (or according to other versions, before) the war with Rāvaṇa, worshipped Śiva here; the liṅga is said to have been made of sand by Sītā (Rāmaliṅgam), while a second liṅga (Viśvaliṅgam) was brought by Hanumān from Kailāsa. The story is told in later retellings and sthala texts, not in the critical text of Vālmīki.

The temple was expanded in the 12th century under the Pāṇḍyas, with sanctum renovations credited to the Āryacakravarti kings of Jaffna; the famous corridors were built mainly under the Sētupati rulers of Ramnad in the 17th–18th centuries.

dates.label: Liṅga worshipped by Rāma (Rāmaliṅga made by Sītā; Viśvaliṅga brought by Hanumān) — temple tradition
dates.basis: temple tradition (sthala-purāṇa / local narrative); not a historical date

name: Aruṇācaleśvara temple, Tiruvannamalai
summary: Large temple at the foot of Aruṇācala hill, worshipped as the fire (agni) liṅga among the five element shrines; the hill itself is identified in tradition with the column of fire of the Liṅgodbhava story.
details: The temple tradition holds that Śiva appeared here as an infinite column of fire to settle the dispute between Brahmā and Viṣṇu; the annual Kārttikai Dīpam lights a beacon on the summit. The present masonry structure goes back to the Cōḻa period (9th c.), with major Vijayanagara and later additions including the thousand-pillared hall and the tall gopuras. Tiruvannamalai is sung in the Tēvāram.

dates.label: Śiva manifested as a column of fire (Liṅgodbhava) at Aruṇācala — sthala tradition

name: Jambukeśvara temple, Thiruvanaikaval
summary: Śiva temple on Srirangam island worshipped as the water (jala) liṅga among the five element shrines; a spring keeps the sanctum floor moist.
details: The temple tradition tells of a spider and an elephant (āṉai, hence the name) that worshipped the liṅga under a jambu tree; the spider was reborn as the early Cōḻa king Kōcceṅkaṇāṉ, credited with building many Śiva temples. The surviving structure is medieval Cōḻa and later. The temple is sung in the Tēvāram.

dates.label: Founded by the early Cōḻa king Kōccēṅkaṇāṉ, reborn from a spider devotee (sthala tradition)

name: Ekāmbareśvara temple, Kanchipuram
summary: Major Śiva temple of Kanchipuram worshipped as the earth (pṛthvī) liṅga among the five element shrines, centred on a sacred mango tree; its southern gopura is among the tallest in South India.
details: The temple tradition holds that Pārvatī made a liṅga of sand beneath a mango tree (ekāmra, “single mango”) and embraced it when Śiva tested her with a flood. The masonry temple goes back to the Cōḻa period, with very large Vijayanagara additions including the thousand-pillared hall and the gopura. It is sung in the Tēvāram.

dates.label: Pārvatī worshipped a sand liṅga under the mango tree (sthala tradition)
dates.basis: temple tradition (sthala-purāṇa / local narrative); not a historical date

name: Kailāsanātha temple, Kanchipuram
summary: Sandstone Śiva temple built by the Pallava king Narasiṃhavarman II Rājasiṃha around 700 CE, with additions by his son Mahendravarman III; one of the earliest large structural temples of Tamil Nadu.
details: The temple is enclosed by a wall lined with small shrine-cells (58 in number) carrying sculpture of Śiva’s forms. Rājasiṃha’s inscriptions on the temple give it his name (Rājasiṃheśvara). The style develops the Drāviḍa vimāna first tried in the Mamallapuram monoliths.

name: Vaikuṇṭha Perumāḷ temple, Kanchipuram
summary: Eighth-century Pallava Viṣṇu temple built by Nandivarman II Pallavamalla, with three superimposed sanctums and a cloister of relief panels that narrate Pallava dynastic history; a Divya Deśam sung by Tirumaṅkai Āḻvār.
details: Originally called Parameśvara-viṇṇakaram (“Viṣṇu-house of Parameśvara”), the temple has sanctums on three levels showing Viṣṇu seated, standing and reclining. The cloister reliefs with labels are an important source for Pallava history, including the accession of Nandivarman II. Tirumaṅkai Āḻvār, a contemporary of the king, praised the temple in the Periya Tirumoḻi. Dating views range from c. 690 to c. 770–775 CE.

dates.label: late 8th c. CE (reign of Nandivarman II, c. 731–796; stylistically c. 770–775)
dates.basis: regnal synchronism, labelled reliefs and style

name: Varadarāja Perumāḷ temple, Kanchipuram
summary: Large Viṣṇu temple of Kanchipuram on the Hastigiri mound, a Divya Deśam closely associated with Rāmānuja; renovated under the Cōḻas from 1053 and expanded by later dynasties.
details: The temple was renovated by the Cōḻas in 1053 and expanded under Kulōttuṅga I and Vikrama Cōḻa; further walls and gopuras were added in the 14th century and later. It is famous for the wooden Atti Varadar image kept submerged in the temple tank and displayed only every 40 years (most recently in 2019).

dates.label: expansion under Kulōttuṅga I and Vikrama Cōḻa

limits: Dates the Cōḻa and later fabric; does not establish the pre-Cōḻa history claimed in tradition.

name: Group of Monuments at Mamallapuram
summary: Seventh- and eighth-century Pallava port with rock-cut cave temples (maṇḍapas), monolithic rathas, open-air reliefs and the structural Shore Temple; a World Heritage property since 1984.
details: Most monuments are attributed to Narasiṃhavarman I Māmalla (c. 630–668), after whom the town is named, with earlier work under Mahendravarman I and later work under Rājasiṃha (Narasiṃhavarman II). The great open-air relief is identified by some scholars as the Descent of the Gaṅgā (Bhagīratha’s penance) and by others as Arjuna’s penance to obtain the Pāśupata weapon; the Mahiṣamardinī cave shows the Goddess battling the buffalo demon and the Kṛṣṇa maṇḍapa shows Kṛṣṇa lifting Govardhana.

dates.label: c. 630–728 CE (Narasiṃhavarman I to Rājasiṃha)
dates.basis: Pallava inscriptions, royal titles carved on monuments and style

location.label: Mamallapuram (Mahabalipuram), Chengalpattu district, Tamil Nadu, India

name: Shore Temple, Mamallapuram
summary: Granite structural temple on the shore at Mamallapuram, built under Narasiṃhavarman II Rājasiṃha around 700–728 CE, combining two Śiva shrines with a shrine of the reclining Viṣṇu.
details: Inscriptions name the shrines Kṣatriyasiṃha-Pallaveśvara-gṛham and Rājasiṃha-Pallaveśvara-gṛham (both Śiva) and a Viṣṇu shrine of Narapatisiṃha, a title of Rājasiṃha. The 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami briefly exposed remains of other structures along the coast.

attributes.unesco: part of Group of Monuments at Mahabalipuram (1984; no. 249)

limits: Dates the structural phase of Pallava building at Mamallapuram; local legends of “seven pagodas” lost to the sea are tradition, only partly paralleled by archaeological finds.

name: Pañca Rathas, Mamallapuram
summary: Five monolithic shrines carved from a single granite outcrop in the 7th century, popularly named after the Pāṇḍavas and Draupadī; they model the main types of early Drāviḍa shrine and were never consecrated.
details: The popular names (Dharmarāja, Bhīma, Arjuna, Nakula–Sahadeva and Draupadī rathas) are later and have no connection with the original dedications. The monuments are usually attributed to Narasiṃhavarman I, although newer readings of inscriptions have suggested work continued into the reign of Rājasiṃha.

name: Subrahmaṇya temple, Tirupparankundram
summary: Rock-cut and structural temple of Murukaṉ on a hill outside Madurai, counted first of the six abodes; tradition places Murukaṉ’s marriage to Deivayāṉai (Devasenā) here.
details: The core is a rock-cut cave shrine converted into a Hindu temple under a minister of a later Pāṇḍya king in the late 8th century CE, with pillared halls added by the Madurai Nāyakas. A separate Pāṇḍya rock-cut Śiva cave lies at the foot of the hill.

summary: Seashore temple of Murukaṉ on the Gulf of Mannar, counted second of the six abodes; tradition places here Murukaṉ’s victory over the demon Śūrapadma, re-enacted in the Skanda Ṣaṣṭhī festival.

summary: Hilltop temple of Murukaṉ as the renunciant Daṇḍāyudhapāṇi, counted third of the six abodes and one of the most visited temples in Tamil Nadu.

name: Guruvāyūr temple
summary: Kerala temple of Kṛṣṇa as Guruvāyūrappaṉ (a four-armed Viṣṇu image worshipped as the child Kṛṣṇa), one of the most visited temples of South India.
details: Tradition holds that the image was installed by Guru (Bṛhaspati) and Vāyu, hence the name. The Nārāyaṇīyam of Mēlputtūr Nārāyaṇa Bhaṭṭatiri (late 16th c.) was composed in the temple. The sanctum murals were damaged in a fire in 1970 and restored in the 1980s. Entry is restricted to Hindus.

name: Padmanābhasvāmī temple, Thiruvananthapuram
summary: Temple of Viṣṇu reclining on Ananta at the heart of Thiruvananthapuram, a Divya Deśam and the tutelary shrine of the Travancore royal house; the opening of its vaults in 2011 revealed a very large treasure.
details: The temple in its present form was rebuilt in the 18th century under Mārtāṇḍa Varma of Travancore, who in 1750 dedicated his kingdom to Padmanābha (the Thṛppaṭidānam). Records of the temple (the Mathilakam records) were kept in a record room built c. 1425. The vault inventory ordered by the Supreme Court of India from 2011 made it internationally known.

dates.label: Ancient foundation praised by Nammāḻvār (tradition and hymns)
dates.basis: temple tradition (sthala-purāṇa / local narrative); not a historical date

dates.label: 18th c. CE rebuilding under Mārtāṇḍa Varma; kingdom dedicated 1750

limits: Dates the 18th-century rebuilding; the treasure is evidence of royal and devotional donation over centuries, not of the temple’s antiquity as such.
openQuestions: Date of the earliest surviving fabric not verified.

name: Veṅkaṭeśvara temple, Tirumala
summary: Hill temple of Veṅkaṭeśvara on the Tirumala range above Tirupati, among the most visited and richest religious institutions in the world; a Divya Deśam sung by the Āḻvārs.
details: The site (Vēṅkaṭam) is named in old Tamil literature and praised by the Āḻvārs. The temple’s epigraphic record, published by the Tirumala Tirupati Devasthanams, includes a Pallava-period gift of a silver image by the queen Sāmavai (966 CE) and very many Vijayanagara grants; Kṛṣṇadevarāya visited repeatedly and on 2 January 1517 installed portrait statues of himself and his queens. The temple has been administered by the TTD under state legislation since the 20th century.

dates.label: Viṣṇu came to Vēṅkaṭam as Śrīnivāsa and married Padmāvatī (Veṅkaṭācala Māhātmya tradition)
dates.basis: temple tradition (sthala-purāṇa / local narrative); not a historical date

dates.label: 966 CE gift of a silver image by the Pallava queen Sāmavai (earliest dated gift commonly cited)
dates.basis: temple inscription as published by TTD (reading not checked here)

dates.label: Vijayanagara grants and portrait statues of Kṛṣṇadevarāya (installed 2 Jan. 1517)

location.label: Tirumala, Tirupati district, Andhra Pradesh, India

limits: Epigraphy shows continuous royal and lay endowment from the 10th century; it does not resolve the tradition’s accounts of the deity’s descent, nor the older sectarian debates over the image’s original identity.

name: Mallikārjuna temple, Srisailam
summary: Fortified hilltop temple above the Krishna gorge that is counted both as a jyotirliṅga (Mallikārjuna) and as a Śakti Pīṭha (Bhramarāmbā); it is also sung in the Tēvāram.
details: Much of the present complex was added under the Vijayanagara kings from the 14th century, and the enclosure walls carry narrative reliefs; a gopura is associated by tradition with Śivājī’s visit in 1677. Wikipedia reports Sātavāhana-period epigraphic references to Śrīparvata; these refer to the hill, not to the standing temple.

dates.label: Śiva and Pārvatī came to Śrīśaila to be near their son Kumāra (Śiva Purāṇa jyotirliṅga account)
dates.basis: temple tradition (sthala-purāṇa / local narrative); not a historical date

dates.label: 14th–16th c. CE Vijayanagara additions (most of the present complex)

location.label: Srisailam, Nandyal district, Andhra Pradesh, India

limits: Early references to Śrīparvata attest the sacred hill, not the present temple; the jyotirliṅga and pīṭha identities are list-based traditions.

name: Śrīkāḷahastīśvara temple, Srikalahasti
summary: Śiva temple on the Svarṇamukhī river worshipped as the air (vāyu) liṅga among the five element shrines and associated with the hunter-saint Kaṇṇappa; it is sung in the Tēvāram.
details: The name combines śrī (spider), kāḷa (serpent) and hasti (elephant), three animal devotees of the temple legend. The main structure is credited to Rājendra Cōḻa I (11th c.), with gopuras of Kulōttuṅga I and large Vijayanagara additions under Kṛṣṇadevarāya (a gopura of 1516).

dates.label: Worshipped by a spider, a serpent and an elephant, and by the hunter Kaṇṇappa (sthala tradition)
dates.basis: temple tradition (sthala-purāṇa / local narrative); not a historical date

dates.label: 11th c. CE Cōḻa main structure (Rājendra I; gopuras of Kulōttuṅga I)

location.label: Srikalahasti, Tirupati district, Andhra Pradesh, India

limits: Dates the Cōḻa and later fabric; the infobox’s 5th-century foundation and the animal-devotee legend are tradition.

name: Paraśurāmeśvara temple, Gudimallam
summary: Village temple near Renigunta whose apsidal sanctum enshrines the Gudimallam liṅga, a realistic liṅga carved with a standing two-armed figure that is among the earliest surviving images connected with Śiva; the liṅga is dated by most scholars between the 2nd/1st c. BCE and the early centuries CE.
details: The liṅga has remained in worship while the temple around it has been rebuilt; the present structure belongs to later centuries (Pallava/Bāṇa to Cōḻa-period inscriptions and later rebuilding), on an earlier apsidal plan. Excavation by I. K. Sarma (ASI) in 1973 investigated the original setting of the liṅga. The temple is ASI-protected.

dates.label: Liṅga worshipped by Paraśurāma (temple name and tradition)
dates.basis: temple tradition (sthala-purāṇa / local narrative); not a historical date

dates.label: liṅga: c. 2nd–1st c. BCE (majority) to 1st–3rd c. CE (some)
dates.basis: style and stratigraphy of the 1973 excavation

dates.label: temple fabric rebuilt c. 9th–13th c. CE on the earlier apsidal plan

location.label: Gudimallam, Tirupati district, Andhra Pradesh, India

limits: The liṅga establishes early worship of a phallic emblem with an anthropomorphic deity (generally read as Śiva/Rudra); its exact date and the identity of the figure remain debated, and the standing temple is much later.

name: Navabrahma temples, Alampur
summary: Group of nine Śiva temples of the Bādāmi Cālukya period (7th–8th c.) near the confluence of the Tuṅgabhadrā and Kṛṣṇā, unusual in the south for their Nāgara (curvilinear) towers; the nearby Jogulāmbā shrine is counted among the eighteen Mahāśakti Pīṭhas.
details: Early 8th-century inscriptions at the site indicate a Śaiva maṭha. Much of the area was re-sited when the Srisailam dam reservoir was created, and the Jogulāmbā temple was rebuilt in modern times.

location.label: Alampur, Jogulamba Gadwal district, Telangana, India

limits: Dates Cālukya patronage of northern-style towers in the Deccan; the Śakti-pīṭha identification of Jogulāmbā belongs to the later eighteen-pīṭha list.

name: Rāmappa (Rudreśvara) temple, Palampet
summary: Kākatīya Śiva temple at Palampet commissioned in 1213 by the general Recherla Rudra under king Gaṇapati; inscribed on the World Heritage List in 2021 and popularly named after its sculptor.
details: A pillar inscription in the courtyard records the commission in 1213; construction is said to have taken about four decades. The temple is known for its bracket figures of dancers and for very light porous bricks used in the superstructure.

attributes.unesco: Kakatiya Rudreshwara (Ramappa) Temple, Telangana — inscribed 2021; UNESCO list no. 1570
attributes.protection: ASI Monument of National Importance (N-TG-5, as listed on Wikipedia)

limits: Dates the temple securely; the naming after the sculptor Rāmappa is local tradition.

name: Bādāmi cave temples
summary: Four rock-cut cave temples (three Hindu, one Jain) in the sandstone cliff of Vātāpi, capital of the early Cālukyas; Cave 3, dedicated to Viṣṇu, carries an inscription of Śaka 500 (578 CE), making it one of the earliest precisely dated Brahmanical cave temples.
details: Cave 1 is Śaiva (with an eighteen-armed dancing Śiva), Caves 2 and 3 are Vaiṣṇava, with large panels of Trivikrama (Vāmana’s three strides), Varāha and Narasiṃha, and Cave 4 is Jain. The Cave 3 inscription records its dedication by Maṅgaleśa in the twelfth regnal year of his brother Kīrtivarman I.
limits: The Cave 3 inscription dates the excavation and royal Vaiṣṇava patronage; the reliefs show which avatāra narratives were current in 6th-c. Karnataka, not their origin.

name: Meguti Jain temple, Aihole
summary: Jain temple on a hill at Aihole whose east wall bears the Aihole praśasti of Pulakeśin II composed by Ravikīrti and dated Śaka 556 (634/635 CE); it is one of the earliest securely dated structural temples in the Deccan.
details: The inscription, in Sanskrit verse, praises Pulakeśin II’s victories (including over Harṣa) and records Ravikīrti’s building of this Jina temple. It is also an early external attestation of the poets Kālidāsa and Bhāravi, whom Ravikīrti names, and dates itself by the Kali era as well as the Śaka era.
limits: The inscription securely dates the temple and Ravikīrti’s patronage; its account of Pulakeśin II’s victories is royal panegyric.

name: Durgā temple, Aihole
summary: Apsidal-ended early Cālukya temple at Aihole (late 7th–early 8th c.) surrounded by a colonnaded ambulatory; its name derives from a later fort (durga) built on it, not from the goddess.
details: The original dedication is debated (Viṣṇu and Sūrya have both been proposed), and the temple has served as a test case for the historiography of early Indian architecture, as Tartakov has shown. Niche sculptures include Narasiṃha, Varāha, Mahiṣamardinī and Śiva.

attributes.architecture: early Cālukya, apsidal plan with Nāgara śikhara

limits: The name “Durgā” is a misnomer from a later fort; the original cult image and dedication are not certainly known.
openQuestions: Original dedication of the sanctum (Viṣṇu or Sūrya).

name: Lāḍ Khān temple, Aihole
summary: Flat-roofed early Cālukya Śiva temple at Aihole, named after a later occupant; its date is a classic problem of Indian architectural history, with proposals ranging from the 5th to the early 8th century.
details: Early surveys (Cousens and others) treated Lāḍ Khān as a 5th-century prototype of the Hindu temple; later scholarship generally moved it to the late 7th or early 8th century on stylistic grounds. The current Wikipedia article reverses this, saying it is “now dated” to the 5th century, with weak sourcing. This dataset records both views as competing.

dates.label: c. 5th c. CE
dates.basis: early typological dating; repeated on Wikipedia

limits: No dedicatory inscription dates the building; any date rests on stylistic comparison.

name: Virūpākṣa temple, Pattadakal
summary: The largest temple at Pattadakal, built c. 740–745 CE by Queen Lokamahādevī to commemorate her husband Vikramāditya II’s victory over the Pallavas; its Drāviḍa design closely follows the Kailāsanātha temple of Kanchipuram.
details: Inscriptions call it the Lokeśvara (after its patron). It was built by a queen of Vikramāditya II after his capture of Kanchipuram, and its style reflects contact with Pallava architecture. The walls carry reliefs from the Rāmāyaṇa and Mahābhārata and Purāṇic themes; the temple remains in worship. The Group of Monuments at Pattadakal was inscribed on the World Heritage List in 1987.

dates.label: c. 740–745 CE
dates.basis: inscriptions of Lokamahādevī and regnal synchronism with Vikramāditya II

attributes.unesco: Group of Monuments at Pattadakal — inscribed 1987; UNESCO list no. 239
attributes.protection: World Heritage property managed by the ASI

limits: Royal inscriptions date the temple and its patron; the commemorated victory is presented from the Cālukya side.

name: Pāpanātha temple, Pattadakal
summary: Mid-8th-century Cālukya Śiva temple at Pattadakal that fuses Nāgara and Drāviḍa elements and is known for its narrative panels from the Rāmāyaṇa and the Kirātārjunīya.
details: The temple stands about half a kilometre south of the main group. The ASI and Michell date it towards the end of early Cālukya rule.

attributes.unesco: part of Group of Monuments at Pattadakal (1987; no. 239)

limits: The reliefs show the circulation of Rāmāyaṇa and Kirātārjunīya narratives in 8th-c. Karnataka; they do not date the narratives themselves.

name: Kailāsa temple (Ellora Cave 16)
summary: A complete Drāviḍa temple carved downward and inward from the basalt hillside at Ellora in the 8th century, generally attributed to the Rāṣṭrakūṭa king Kṛṣṇa I (r. c. 756–773); its form evokes Mount Kailāsa, Śiva’s abode.
details: The temple has no dedicatory inscription. Its attribution rests on later epigraphs: the Baroda (Vadodara) copper plates of Karkarāja II (812 CE) praise a marvellous temple built by Kṛṣṇarāja at Elāpura that astonished even its architect, and another grant similarly credits Kṛṣṇarāja. The best-known relief shows Rāvaṇa shaking Kailāsa while Śiva steadies it with his toe; the walls also carry long Rāmāyaṇa and Mahābhārata friezes. Ellora was inscribed as a World Heritage property in 1983.

dates.label: c. 756–773 CE (main excavation, reign of Kṛṣṇa I), with later elements
dates.basis: later copper-plate inscriptions crediting Kṛṣṇarāja; no dedicatory inscription

location.label: Ellora (Verul), Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar district, Maharashtra, India

attributes.unesco: Ellora Caves — inscribed 1983; UNESCO list no. 243
attributes.protection: World Heritage property managed by the ASI

limits: Attribution to Kṛṣṇa I is inferred from inscriptions of his successors; the Rāvaṇa relief is evidence for the narrative’s popularity, not for its events.

name: Daśāvatāra cave (Ellora Cave 15)
summary: Two-storeyed rock-cut temple at Ellora whose plan follows the Buddhist vihāras nearby but whose sculpture is Śaiva and Vaiṣṇava; an inscription of the Rāṣṭrakūṭa founder Dantidurga on the back wall of the front maṇḍapa is key to its date.
details: The cave was probably begun as a Buddhist excavation and completed as a Hindu temple. The Dantidurga inscription places its completion in the mid-8th century, just before the Kailāsa.

attributes.unesco: part of Ellora Caves (1983; no. 243)

sources.locator: infobox coordinates of the Ellora group

limits: Coordinates are those of the Ellora group, not the individual cave.

name: Elephanta Caves (Cave 1)
summary: Great Śiva cave on Elephanta island in Mumbai harbour, completed in the mid-6th century, whose colossal three-headed Sadāśiva (Maheśamūrti) is among the masterpieces of Indian sculpture.
details: Cave 1 has a pillared hall with a free-standing liṅga shrine and large relief panels: Sadāśiva, Ardhanārīśvara, Gaṅgādhara, the marriage of Śiva and Pārvatī, Rāvaṇa shaking Kailāsa, Andhakāntaka and Naṭarāja. Most scholars date its completion to the second quarter of the 6th century; the patron is unknown, with the Kalacuri king Kṛṣṇarāja among the candidates. The Portuguese named the island after a stone elephant found there. Inscribed as a World Heritage property in 1987.

location.label: Elephanta Island, Raigad district (Mumbai harbour), Maharashtra, India

attributes.unesco: Elephanta Caves — inscribed 1987; UNESCO list no. 244
attributes.protection: World Heritage property managed by the ASI

limits: There is no foundation inscription; patron and exact date are inferred. The panels document 6th-c. Śaiva iconography, not the antiquity of the myths.
openQuestions: Patron: Kalacuri, Maurya of Konkan, or other — unresolved.

name: Virūpākṣa temple, Hampi
summary: Living Śiva temple of Virūpākṣa–Pampāpati on the Tuṅgabhadrā at Hampi, whose small early shrine was enlarged into a vast complex under the Vijayanagara kings; it predates and outlived the imperial city.
details: The shrine core is early (7th c. per some accounts), and the tutelary god Virūpākṣa became the patron deity of the Vijayanagara rulers. The great complex was built by Lakkaṇa Daṇḍeśa, a chief under Devarāya II, and Kṛṣṇadevarāya commissioned the ranga-maṇḍapa in 1510 to mark his accession. Worship continued after the sack of the city in 1565.

dates.label: Pampā (Pārvatī) won Śiva by penance at Hampi (sthala tradition)
dates.basis: temple tradition (sthala-purāṇa / local narrative); not a historical date

dates.label: early shrine core (7th c. per secondary sources) with pre-Vijayanagara additions
major enlargement under Devarāya II (by Lakkaṇa Daṇḍeśa)

attributes.unesco: part of Group of Monuments at Hampi (1986; no. 241)

limits: Dates the stages of royal building; the tradition of Pampā’s penance is local mythology.

name: Hazāra Rāma temple, Hampi
summary: Royal chapel of the Vijayanagara palace zone dedicated to Rāma, whose outer and inner walls are covered with friezes of the Rāmāyaṇa and of royal processions; it is attributed to Devarāya I in the early 15th century.
details: The temple, known in inscriptions as the Rāmacandra temple, sits at the centre of the royal enclosure. Its narrative panels follow the story from Daśaratha’s sacrifice to the war with Rāvaṇa, and outer friezes show the Mahānavamī festival. Dallapiccola, Fritz, Michell and Rajasekhara published the full sculptural programme (1992).

dates.label: early 15th c. CE (attributed to Devarāya I)
dates.basis: inscription and style as discussed by Dallapiccola et al.

attributes.unesco: part of Group of Monuments at Hampi (1986; no. 241)

limits: The friezes are evidence for the Rāmāyaṇa’s role in Vijayanagara royal ideology; they say nothing about the historicity of Rāma.

name: Vijaya Viṭṭhala temple, Hampi
summary: Vijayanagara temple of Viṭṭhala (a form of Viṣṇu/Kṛṣṇa worshipped at Pandharpur) at Hampi, famous for its “musical” pillars and the stone chariot that serves as Garuḍa’s shrine; mostly built in the 15th–16th centuries, with major additions under Kṛṣṇadevarāya.
details: The temple complex sits within a bazaar street in the north-east of the city. Its halls were expanded in the early 16th century; the stone ratha in the courtyard is a Garuḍa shrine. It has not been in worship since the city’s fall in 1565.

dates.label: 15th–16th c. CE, with major expansion under Kṛṣṇadevarāya (1509–1529)

attributes.unesco: part of Group of Monuments at Hampi (1986; no. 241)

limits: The monument dates Vijayanagara devotion to Viṭṭhala; it does not establish when the Pandharpur cult began.

name: Cennakeśava temple, Belur
summary: Hoysaḷa temple of Viṣṇu as Cennakeśava commissioned by King Viṣṇuvardhana in 1117 CE at his early capital Belur; its bracket figures and lathe-turned pillars are hallmarks of the Hoysaḷa style.
details: The temple is still in worship. The dedication date of 1117 is given in inscriptions at the site, and the work continued for decades under Viṣṇuvardhana’s successors. With Halebidu and Somanathapura it forms the Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas World Heritage property (2023).

attributes.unesco: Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas — inscribed 2023; UNESCO list no. 1670

limits: Securely dated royal Vaiṣṇava foundation; later traditions that link it to Rāmānuja’s influence on Viṣṇuvardhana are hagiographic.

name: Hoysaḷeśvara temple, Halebidu
summary: Twin-shrined Śiva temple at the Hoysaḷa capital Dvārasamudra (Halebidu), begun c. 1121 under Viṣṇuvardhana by his officer Ketamalla; its friezes carry thousands of sculptures including Rāmāyaṇa, Mahābhārata and Bhāgavata scenes.
details: An inscription found near the Kalleśvara ruins at Ghattadahalli records Ketamalla’s construction. The city was sacked by Delhi Sultanate armies in the early 14th century. Part of the Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas (2023).

attributes.unesco: Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas — inscribed 2023; UNESCO list no. 1670

limits: Dates the temple; the narrative friezes attest which epic and Purāṇic stories were current in 12th-c. Karnataka.

name: Keśava temple, Somanathapura
summary: Triple-shrined (trikūṭa) Hoysaḷa Viṣṇu temple on a star-shaped plan, consecrated by Somanātha Daṇḍanāyaka, a general of Narasiṃha III; Wikipedia gives 1258 CE while many guides give 1268.
details: The town is named after the patron. The temple is not in worship. Part of the Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas (2023).

dates.label: 1268 CE
dates.basis: date widely repeated in guidebooks; an entrance inscription of c. 1268 is reported

attributes.unesco: Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas — inscribed 2023; UNESCO list no. 1670

limits: The patron is secure; the exact year (1258 or 1268) needs a check against the published inscription (Epigraphia Carnatica).
openQuestions: 1258 vs 1268: Narasiṃha III’s accession is usually placed in 1263, which sits awkwardly with 1258.

name: Śiva temple, Ambarnath
summary: Bhūmija-style Śiva temple near Mumbai bearing an inscription of 1060 CE from the Śilāhāra period, one of the best-preserved 11th-century temples of the northern Konkan.
details: Wikipedia states that it was probably built by the Śilāhāra king Chittarāja and possibly rebuilt by his son Mummuṇi (Māmvāṇi). The temple is ASI-protected.
limits: The inscription dates the building; attribution to a particular Śilāhāra king is less certain.

name: Bhīmaśaṅkara temple
summary: Śiva temple in the Sahyādri forest at the source of the Bhīmā river, claimed as the Bhīmaśaṅkara jyotirliṅga (a claim also made for sites in Assam and elsewhere).
details: The black-stone temple goes back to around the 13th century; its hall and śikhara were improved in the 18th century under Nānā Phaḍṇavīs.

dates.label: 18th c. CE additions under Nānā Phaḍṇavīs

limits: The fabric dates the present temple; its jyotirliṅga status rests on traditional lists and does not date the cult.

name: Tryambakeśvara temple
summary: Jyotirliṅga temple near the source of the Godāvarī in the Brahmagiri hills, whose liṅga is a hollow with three small lingas (Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva); the present temple was built by the Peshwa Bāḷājī Bājīrāv in the mid-18th century.
details: The Kuśāvarta tank in the precinct is regarded as the ritual source of the Godāvarī. Trimbak is one of the sites of the Kumbha Melā (with Nashik).
limits: The fabric dates the present temple; its jyotirliṅga status rests on traditional lists and does not date the cult.

name: Ghṛṣṇeśvara temple
summary: Jyotirliṅga temple near Ellora, restored by Mālojī Bhosale in the 16th century and rebuilt in its present red-stone form in the 18th century under Holkar patronage.
details: Sources differ on the 18th-century patron: Wikipedia names Gautamābāī Holkar (rebuilding of 1729), while many accounts credit Ahilyābāī Holkar. The Śiva Purāṇa names the twelfth jyotirliṅga Ghuśmeśa after the devotee Ghuśmā.

dates.label: Ghuśmā’s devotion restored her son, and Śiva remained as Ghuśmeśa (Śiva Purāṇa)
dates.basis: temple tradition (sthala-purāṇa / local narrative); not a historical date

dates.label: 16th c. CE restoration by Mālojī Bhosale
18th c. CE rebuilding under Holkar patronage
dates.basis: secondary accounts differ (1729 Gautamābāī Holkar vs Ahilyābāī Holkar)

location.label: Verul (Ellora), Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar district, Maharashtra, India

limits: The fabric dates the present temple; its jyotirliṅga status rests on traditional lists and does not date the cult.

name: Vaijanātha temple, Parli
summary: Śiva temple at Parli in Marathwada, one of the candidates for the Vaidyanātha jyotirliṅga (the other main claimant being Deoghar in Jharkhand).
details: The present Hemāḍpanthī-style temple was renovated in 1706 according to Wikipedia; many accounts credit Ahilyābāī Holkar with later work.
limits: The fabric dates the present temple; its jyotirliṅga status rests on traditional lists and does not date the cult.

name: Nāganātha temple, Aundha
summary: Hemāḍpanthī-style Śiva temple in Marathwada claimed as the Nāgeśvara jyotirliṅga, one of three competing claimants (with Dwarka and Jageshwar).
details: Local tradition attributes the first temple to Yudhiṣṭhira during the Pāṇḍavas’ exile. The surviving fabric is medieval (often assigned to the Seuṇa/Yādava period, 13th c.), with 18th-century renovation by Ahilyābāī Holkar.

dates.label: Built by Yudhiṣṭhira during the exile (local tradition)
dates.basis: temple tradition (sthala-purāṇa / local narrative); not a historical date

dates.label: c. 13th c. CE (Seuṇa period, by style)
18th c. CE renovation by Ahilyābāī Holkar

limits: The fabric dates the present temple; its jyotirliṅga status rests on traditional lists and does not date the cult.

name: Udayagiri caves (Vidiśā)
summary: Group of about twenty rock-cut shrines near Vidiśā excavated under the Gupta king Candragupta II, the only cave site securely tied to a Gupta monarch by inscriptions; Cave 5 holds the monumental relief of Varāha raising the Earth.
details: An inscription in Cave 6 is dated Gupta year 82 (c. 401/402 CE) in the reign of Candragupta II, and a Jain cave (Cave 20) has an inscription of 425/426 CE. Besides the Varāha panel, the caves include an early Mahiṣāsuramardinī, a reclining Viṣṇu, river goddesses and ekamukha-liṅgas. Scholars have read the Varāha panel as a political allegory of the Gupta king rescuing the earth (Williams; Willis), a reading that remains interpretive. The site is ASI-protected, close to Besnagar, findspot of the Heliodorus pillar.

sources.locator: CII III, Udayagiri cave inscription of Candragupta II, year 82

dates.label: late 4th–early 5th c. CE (main Hindu caves); Jain cave 425/426 CE

location.label: Udayagiri, Vidisha district, Madhya Pradesh, India

limits: Establishes Gupta royal patronage of Vaiṣṇava, Śaiva and Śākta imagery around 400 CE; the political reading of the Varāha panel is scholarly interpretation, and the panel does not date the Varāha myth.

name: Daśāvatāra temple, Deogarh
summary: Late Gupta stone temple of Viṣṇu (c. 500–550 CE) on the Betwā, one of the earliest surviving North Indian temples with a tower; its wall panels show Viṣṇu reclining on Śeṣa, Gajendra-mokṣa and Nara-Nārāyaṇa.
details: The temple stands on a raised terrace and originally had four corner shrines (pañcāyatana plan). Its name is modern; the iconography is Vaiṣṇava throughout. Cunningham reported Gupta-script inscriptions in the area. The site is ASI-protected.

location.label: Deogarh, Lalitpur district, Uttar Pradesh, India

limits: Undated by inscription; the panels attest Vaiṣṇava narrative iconography around 500 CE.

name: Pārvatī temple, Nachna
summary: Early stone temple at Nachna with a sanctum surrounded by a covered ambulatory and an upper chamber, carved with rock-like rustication; dated by style to the 5th or 6th century.
details: The Pārvatī temple is one of the Nachna group in Panna district. After Cunningham’s visit its upper cella collapsed and was later reconstructed. The nearby Caturmukha Mahādeva temple is later (9th c.). Its exact date and dedication are debated.

location.label: Nachna, Panna district, Madhya Pradesh, India

attributes.architecture: early Gupta-period flat-roofed type with upper chamber

limits: Undated by inscription; current name may not reflect the original dedication.

name: Bhitargaon brick temple
summary: Late 5th-century Gupta-period brick temple near Kanpur, the oldest surviving roofed brick/terracotta Hindu shrine with a high śikhara; its terracotta panels include Viṣṇu and other Purāṇic subjects.
details: The temple is built on a square plan with double-recessed corners and faces east; its upper chamber was damaged in the 18th century. It is ASI-protected.

location.label: Bhitargaon, Kanpur Nagar district, Uttar Pradesh, India

limits: Undated by inscription; the original dedication is inferred from the terracotta programme.

name: Kaṅkālī Devī temple, Tigawa
summary: Small flat-roofed Gupta-period temple (c. 400–425 CE) with a pillared porch, one of the earliest structural Hindu temples to survive; the doorway shows the river goddesses Gaṅgā and Yamunā.
details: The site once had dozens of temples. The surviving shrine is now worshipped as Kaṅkālī Devī; its original dedication is thought to have been Vaiṣṇava (Narasiṃha imagery is reported), with Cāmuṇḍā images also present.

location.label: Tigawa, Katni district, Madhya Pradesh, India

limits: Undated by inscription; current name reflects later worship.

name: Muṇḍeśvarī temple
summary: Octagonal stone temple on a hill in Kaimur district, Bihar, worshipped for Muṇḍeśvarī and a four-faced liṅga; it is often promoted as the oldest functioning Hindu temple (108 CE), a date most historians of architecture reject.
details: An inscription found in the debris mentions year 30 of an unstated era and a Mahārāja Udayasena. Read in the Śaka era it would give 108 CE, the date displayed by the ASI and the Bihar State Religious Trust Board; read in the Harṣa era it gives 636 CE, and Neuss argues from palaeography for c. 570–590 CE. Architectural historians generally date the existing sculpture to the 6th–7th century, and Buckee has argued that the octagonal shrine itself may be a 16th–17th-century reconstruction reusing earlier doorways and mouldings.

dates.label: 108 CE (if the inscription’s year 30 is Śaka)
dates.view: ASI site plaque / Bihar State Religious Trust Board

dates.label: present octagonal shrine possibly 16th–17th c., reusing 7th-c. members

limits: The inscription’s era is not stated, so its year cannot by itself date the temple; the “oldest functioning temple” claim rests on one reading.

name: Lakṣmaṇa temple, Sirpur
summary: Brick temple at Sirpur (Śrīpura) in Chhattisgarh with a well-preserved śikhara and stone doorframe, the earliest dated monument of the Sirpur group (c. 595–605 CE per Wikipedia; other accounts c. 650).
details: The temple is associated with the Pāṇḍuvaṃśī rulers of Dakṣiṇa Kosala; tradition credits its construction to Queen Vāsaṭā, mother of Mahāśivagupta Bālārjuna, in memory of her husband. Its brick śikhara is among the best surviving examples of early brick temple architecture.

dates.label: c. 595–650 CE
dates.basis: inscription and style (sources differ within this range)

limits: Coordinates are those of the Sirpur group; the attribution to Queen Vāsaṭā rests on an inscription read in secondary literature not checked here.

name: Kandarīya Mahādeva temple, Khajuraho
summary: The largest and most elaborate of the Khajuraho temples, a Śiva temple of c. 1025–1050 CE built under the Candela king Vidyādhara, whose clustered śikhara rises like a mountain range.
details: The temple’s tower is built of 84 miniature spires, and its walls carry some 870 figures, including the celebrated mithuna (erotic) groups. Its construction is placed in the reign of Vidyādhara (r. c. 1003–1035) and slightly after.

location.label: Khajuraho, Chhatarpur district, Madhya Pradesh, India

attributes.unesco: Khajuraho Group of Monuments — inscribed 1986; UNESCO list no. 240
attributes.protection: World Heritage property managed by the ASI

limits: Attribution to Vidyādhara is by regnal synchronism, not by a dedicatory inscription.

name: Lakṣmaṇa temple, Khajuraho
summary: Candela temple of Vaikuṇṭha Viṣṇu completed by Yaśovarman (Lakṣavarman) and dated by an inscription of Vikrama 1011 (953/954 CE), the earliest securely dated of the great Khajuraho temples.
details: The 49-verse Sanskrit inscription, issued in the reign of Dhaṅga, gives the Candela genealogy from Nannuka and records that Yaśovarman built a temple for an image of Vaikuṇṭha that had come from Kailāsa via the Śāhi king of Kabul and the Pratīhāra Herambapāla/Devapāla. The four-headed (three visible) Vaikuṇṭha image reflects Pāñcarātra theology.

location.label: Khajuraho, Chhatarpur district, Madhya Pradesh, India

attributes.unesco: Khajuraho Group of Monuments — inscribed 1986; UNESCO list no. 240
attributes.protection: World Heritage property managed by the ASI

limits: The inscription dates the temple and recounts the image’s route as told by the Candela court; the route itself is not independently confirmed.

name: Sun Temple, Konark
summary: Colossal 13th-century temple of Sūrya conceived as the Sun god’s chariot with 24 carved wheels and seven horses, built c. 1250 under the Eastern Gaṅga king Narasiṃhadeva I; the tower collapsed, and the surviving jagamohana is the largest standing part.
details: European sailors called it the “Black Pagoda”. The main vimāna, estimated at about 70 m, had fallen by the 19th century (Wikipedia notes 1837); in 1903 the jagamohana was filled with sand and sealed to stabilise it. The cause of the destruction is disputed. The wheels are often described as sundials. Inscribed as a World Heritage property in 1984.

dates.label: c. 1250 CE (reign of Narasiṃhadeva I, 1238–1264)
dates.basis: Eastern Gaṅga copper plates and regnal synchronism

dates.label: 1903 CE: jagamohana filled with sand and sealed

attributes.unesco: Sun Temple, Konârak — inscribed 1984; UNESCO list no. 246
attributes.protection: ASI Monument of National Importance N-OR-63 (per Wikipedia); World Heritage property

limits: Establishes royal Saura patronage in 13th-c. Odisha; the temple is a monument, not in worship.

name: Jagannātha temple, Puri
summary: Temple of Jagannātha with Balabhadra and Subhadrā, worshipped in wooden images periodically renewed (Navakalevara), at Puri; the present temple was begun by the Eastern Gaṅga king Anantavarman Coḍagaṅga in the 12th century, and Puri is the eastern dhāma of the Char Dham.
details: The temple chronicle (Mādaḷā Pāñji) attributes the first temple to the legendary king Indradyumna. The present tower was begun under Anantavarman Coḍagaṅga (r. c. 1078–1147/50) and is usually said to have been completed under his successors; Wikipedia’s infobox gives 1161. The annual Rathayātrā carries the deities through the town. Caitanya lived in Puri for his last two decades (1510–1533), and singing of Jayadeva’s Gītagovinda became part of the temple’s ritual. Entry is restricted to Hindus.

dates.label: First temple built by King Indradyumna (Mādaḷā Pāñji / Puruṣottama-māhātmya tradition)
dates.basis: temple tradition (sthala-purāṇa / local narrative); not a historical date

dates.label: begun under Anantavarman Coḍagaṅga, early–mid 12th c.; completion given as 1161 in Wikipedia’s infobox
dates.basis: Eastern Gaṅga copper plates and regnal synchronism

dates.label: late 16th c.: re-establishment of worship and new images under Rāmacandra Deva I of Khurda

limits: The 12th-century temple dates the imperial cult; it does not settle the deity’s origins, which are debated (tribal/Śabara, Vaiṣṇava, Buddhist and Jain hypotheses).

name: Liṅgarāja temple, Bhubaneswar
summary: The largest temple of Bhubaneswar (Ekāmra Kṣetra), an 11th-century Kaliṅga-style Śiva temple whose deity is worshipped as Harihara (Śiva–Viṣṇu); it is attributed to Somavaṃśī kings with later Gaṅga additions.
details: Some accounts credit Yayāti I (11th c.); others the Somavaṃśī line generally, with the bhoga-maṇḍapa and other halls added under the Eastern Gaṅgas, during whose rule the Jagannātha cult gained prominence. The Bindusāgara tank lies to the north. Entry is restricted to Hindus.

dates.label: 11th c. CE (main deuḷa)
dates.basis: style and regnal attribution to Somavaṃśī kings

dates.label: 12th–13th c. CE halls added under the Eastern Gaṅgas

limits: Royal attributions vary in the sources; the temple documents a Śaiva–Vaiṣṇava (Harihara) theology in 11th–13th-c. Odisha.

name: Mukteśvara temple, Bhubaneswar
summary: Small 10th-century Kaliṅga-style Śiva temple in Bhubaneswar (c. 950–975 CE), celebrated for its arched gateway (toraṇa) and refined carving, marking the transition to the mature Odishan style.
details: Most scholars place it after the Paraśurāmeśvara and before the Brahmeśvara (1060 CE); Panigrahi proposed c. 966 under the Somavaṃśī Yayāti I.
limits: Undated by inscription; the date is stylistic.

name: Causaṭh Yoginī temple, Hirapur
summary: Small circular, roofless (hypaethral) sandstone shrine near Bhubaneswar housing images of sixty-four yoginīs around a central Kālī/Mahāmāyā, dated to the 9th century and associated with the Bhauma-Kara queen Hīrādevī.
details: Circular yoginī temples are a distinctive tantric building type found in Odisha and central India. The attribution to Hīrādevī (c. 864 CE per Wikipedia) is traditional.

dates.label: 9th–10th c. CE (traditionally c. 864 under Queen Hīrādevī)

limits: Evidence of a tantric yoginī cult in early medieval Odisha; patronage by Hīrādevī is not inscriptionally confirmed here.

name: Kāmākhyā temple, Guwahati
summary: Principal temple of the goddess Kāmākhyā on Nīlācala hill, Guwahati, where an aniconic yoni-shaped stone in a cave is worshipped; one of the oldest centres of tantric Śākta practice and a Śakti Pīṭha in all major lists. The present temple was rebuilt in 1565 under the Koch king Naranārāyaṇa by his brother Chilarai.
details: The stone base of an earlier Kāmarūpa-period temple survives; a brick śikhara was added in the Koch reconstruction. An inscription in the temple records that Chilarai built it in 1565 in the reign of Naranārāyaṇa (Wikipedia, citing Sarkar 1992). The older story that the Bengal general Kālāpāhāḍ destroyed the temple is now doubted, since the reconstruction precedes his campaign; destruction during Husain Shah’s invasion of Kamata (1498) is suggested instead. The Ahom kings were later patrons. The annual Ambuvācī Melā marks the goddess’s menstruation.

dates.label: Place where Satī’s yoni fell (Kālikā Purāṇa and pīṭha traditions)
dates.basis: temple tradition (sthala-purāṇa / local narrative); not a historical date

dates.label: 1565 CE reconstruction by Chilarai under Naranārāyaṇa
dates.basis: dated temple inscription (as cited by Wikipedia from Sarkar 1992)

attributes.architecture: Nīlācala type (Kāmarūpa stone base with Koch brick superstructure)

limits: The 1565 inscription dates the rebuilding; the site’s older history is inferred from the earlier stone base and Kāmarūpa-period records. The pīṭha identity is mythic tradition.

name: Kālīghāṭ temple, Kolkata
summary: Temple of Kālī on the old course of the Hooghly (Ādi Gaṅgā) in Kolkata, counted as a Śakti Pīṭha where the toes of Satī’s right foot fell; the present building was completed in 1809 under the Sābarṇa Rāy Caudhurī family.
details: Construction of the present temple began in 1798 under Santosh Roy Chowdhury and was completed in 1809. Kālīghāṭ gave its name to a 19th-century school of popular painting.

dates.label: Toes of Satī’s right foot fell here (pīṭha tradition)
dates.basis: temple tradition (sthala-purāṇa / local narrative); not a historical date

limits: The present building is early 19th century; earlier shrines are known only from tradition and texts.

name: Dakṣiṇeśvar Kālī temple
summary: Navaratna-style temple of Kālī as Bhavatāriṇī on the Hooghly north of Kolkata, founded by Rāṇī Rāsmaṇi and consecrated on 31 May 1855; Rāmakṛṣṇa served as its priest.
details: The complex also has twelve Śiva shrines and a Rādhā–Kṛṣṇa temple along the river.

location.label: Dakshineswar, North 24 Parganas, West Bengal, India

limits: A documented 19th-century foundation; included as a modern reference point for Bengal Śākta temple building.

name: Viṣṇupada temple, Gaya
summary: Temple at Gaya enshrining a footprint of Viṣṇu in basalt, central to the śrāddha rites for ancestors performed at Gaya; the present temple was rebuilt in 1787 by Ahilyābāī Holkar.
details: Temple tradition links the site to Viṣṇu’s subduing of the demon Gayāsura. Gaya as a place of ancestral rites is described in the Gayā-māhātmya sections of the Vāyu Purāṇa.

dates.label: Viṣṇu pressed the demon Gayāsura underground, leaving his footprint (Gayā-māhātmya tradition)
dates.basis: temple tradition (sthala-purāṇa / local narrative); not a historical date

limits: The present temple is 18th century; the footprint’s cult is older but undated here.

name: Baidyanātha temple, Deoghar
summary: Complex of 22 temples at Deoghar in Jharkhand, the most widely accepted claimant to the Vaidyanātha jyotirliṅga and also claimed as a Śakti Pīṭha; the month of Śrāvaṇa brings very large kāṃvaṛ pilgrimages carrying Gaṅgā water.
details: Local tradition links the liṅga to Rāvaṇa, who was carrying it to Laṅkā when he was obliged to set it down here. The dates of the present buildings were not verified in this pass.

dates.label: Liṅga set down by Rāvaṇa on his way to Laṅkā (local tradition)
dates.basis: temple tradition (sthala-purāṇa / local narrative); not a historical date

dates.label: present main temple probably 16th–18th c. (not verified)

limits: The jyotirliṅga identification is contested with Parli (Maharashtra) and Baijnath (Himachal); the building date is unverified.
openQuestions: Date and patron of the present main temple.

name: Kāśī Viśvanātha temple, Varanasi
summary: Temple of Śiva as Viśvanātha (Viśveśvara), “Lord of the Universe”, at Varanasi, one of the twelve jyotirliṅgas; the present temple was built in 1780 by Ahilyābāī Holkar on a site adjacent to the earlier temple.
details: The temple has been rebuilt several times. A reconstruction associated with Rāja Todar Mal in 1585 was demolished on the order of the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb in 1669, and the Gyānvāpī mosque stands on that site. Ahilyābāī Holkar of Indore built the present temple nearby in 1780, and in 1835 Mahārājā Ranjit Singh donated gold to plate its tower. A large redevelopment, the Kashi Vishwanath Dham corridor linking the temple to the Gaṅgā, was inaugurated on 13 December 2021. The temple is administered by the Shri Kashi Vishwanath Temple Trust under the Government of Uttar Pradesh.

dates.label: Kāśī as Śiva’s eternal city, never abandoned by him (Kāśī-khaṇḍa tradition)
dates.basis: temple tradition (sthala-purāṇa / local narrative); not a historical date

limits: The present fabric is 18th century; the antiquity of Viśveśvara worship is attested by texts and earlier rebuildings, not by the standing building.

name: Somanātha temple, Prabhas Patan
summary: Seashore Śiva temple at Prabhāsa Pāṭan, first of the twelve jyotirliṅgas in the Śiva Purāṇa list; repeatedly destroyed and rebuilt, the present temple in Māru-Gurjara (Cālukya) style was completed in 1951.
details: Mahmud of Ghazni raided the temple in January 1026 during the reign of the Caulukya king Bhīma I, an event remembered very differently in Persian, Sanskrit and Jain sources, as Romila Thapar has shown. The temple was rebuilt and damaged several more times; Ahilyābāī Holkar built a separate temple nearby in 1783. After Independence, reconstruction on the old site was initiated by Vallabhbhai Patel, and the new temple was inaugurated in May 1951 by President Rajendra Prasad. It is managed by the Shree Somnath Trust.

dates.label: Liṅga established by Soma (the Moon) to be freed from Dakṣa’s curse (Śiva Purāṇa / Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa tradition)
dates.basis: temple tradition (sthala-purāṇa / local narrative); not a historical date

name: Dvārakādhīśa temple, Dwarka
summary: Temple of Kṛṣṇa as “King of Dvārakā” at Dwarka on the Gujarat coast, the western dhāma of the Char Dham and a Divya Deśam; the present five-storeyed structure dates from the 15th–16th centuries.
details: Tradition holds that the first shrine was built by Vajranābha, Kṛṣṇa’s great-grandson, over Kṛṣṇa’s palace. Archaeological work near the temple has found earlier occupation, and offshore explorations have been interpreted by some as Kṛṣṇa’s submerged city, a claim not accepted by most archaeologists. The Dvārakā Śāradā Pīṭha maṭha is associated with Śaṅkara in tradition.

dates.label: First shrine built by Vajranābha, great-grandson of Kṛṣṇa (temple tradition)

limits: The present building is late medieval; the identification of modern Dwarka with the epic Dvārakā is tradition, and offshore finds do not establish the epic city.

name: Nāgeśvara temple, Dwarka
summary: Śiva temple between Dwarka and Bet Dwarka promoted as the Nāgeśvara jyotirliṅga, one of three competing claimants (with Aundha in Maharashtra and Jageshwar in Uttarakhand).
details: The present temple with its large seated Śiva statue is largely a late-20th-century reconstruction (not precisely dated in this pass). The Śiva Purāṇa places Nāgeśa in the Dārukā forest, whose location is disputed.

dates.label: Śiva protected his devotee Supriya from the demon Dāruka in the Dārukā forest (Śiva Purāṇa)
dates.basis: temple tradition (sthala-purāṇa / local narrative); not a historical date

name: Sun temple, Modhera
summary: Caulukya (Solaṅkī) temple of Sūrya at Modhera with a stepped tank (Sūrya Kuṇḍa) and a detached dance hall; its shrine was built in the reign of Bhīma I, shortly after 1026–27 CE.
details: An inscription on the cella wall reads Vikrama Saṃvat 1083 (1026–27 CE); it is placed upside down and is read by most scholars as marking destruction or the start of construction rather than a dedication. The dance hall and tank were added later, perhaps under Karṇa I. The temple is ASI-protected and not in worship.

name: Mahākāleśvara temple, Ujjain
summary: Jyotirliṅga temple of Śiva as Mahākāla in Ujjain, whose south-facing (dakṣiṇāmūrti) liṅga is worshipped with the dawn bhasma-ārati; the present temple is an 18th-century Marāṭhā-period reconstruction.
details: Ujjain’s Mahākāla is celebrated in classical Sanskrit literature, including Kālidāsa’s Meghadūta. The earlier temple complex was destroyed by Iltutmish during his raid of 1234–35. It was rebuilt under Marāṭhā rule in the 18th century, credited by Wikipedia to the diwan Rāmacandra Sukthankar of the Śinde (Scindia) administration. A large precinct development (Mahakal Lok) was opened in 2022.

dates.label: Śiva appeared as Mahākāla to destroy the demon Dūṣaṇa and protect Avantī (Śiva Purāṇa)
dates.basis: temple tradition (sthala-purāṇa / local narrative); not a historical date

limits: The present fabric is 18th century; earlier phases are known from texts and chronicles.

name: Oṃkāreśvara temple
summary: Jyotirliṅga temple on the island of Māndhātā in the Narmadā, whose island is said to resemble the syllable Om; the jyotirliṅga is shared in tradition with the Amaleśvara (Mamaleśvara) temple on the south bank.
details: Wikipedia states the temple was built by Paramāra kings in the 11th century and rebuilt by the Holkars in the 18th century. The Śiva Purāṇa’s list names “Oṃkāre Parameśvaram”, read by some as the Amaleśvara shrine.

location.label: Mandhata island, Khandwa district, Madhya Pradesh, India

limits: Which of the two shrines (Oṃkāreśvara or Amaleśvara) is the jyotirliṅga is itself a matter of local tradition.

name: Bhojeśvara temple, Bhojpur
summary: Unfinished 11th-century Śiva temple at Bhojpur near Bhopal attributed to the Paramāra king Bhoja, housing one of the largest liṅgas in India; construction drawings engraved on the surrounding rock show how the temple was to be completed.
details: Because the temple was never completed it has no dedicatory inscription; the attribution to Bhoja (r. c. 1010–1055) rests on the town’s name and context. The engraved architectural drawings and the earthen ramp used to raise stones make it an important document of medieval building technique.

location.label: Bhojpur, Raisen district, Madhya Pradesh, India

limits: Attribution to Bhoja is circumstantial; the site documents construction technique.

name: Brahmā temple, Pushkar
summary: Temple of Brahmā beside the sacred lake of Puṣkara in Rajasthan, among the very few temples in India dedicated to Brahmā; the present structure dates from the 14th century with later rebuilding.
details: Puṣkara is praised as a tīrtha in the Mahābhārata, and the Padma Purāṇa tells of Brahmā’s sacrifice there. Temple tradition says that Sāvitrī cursed Brahmā to be worshipped only at Puṣkara after he took Gāyatrī as consort for the rite.

dates.label: Brahmā performed a sacrifice at Puṣkara; Sāvitrī’s curse restricts his worship (Padma Purāṇa and temple tradition)
dates.basis: temple tradition (sthala-purāṇa / local narrative); not a historical date

limits: The building is late medieval; the lake’s sanctity is attested much earlier in texts.

name: Rām Mandir, Ayodhya
summary: Temple of Rāma in Ayodhya, Uttar Pradesh, built in the Nāgara (Māru-Gurjara) style after the Supreme Court of India’s judgment of 9 November 2019 and consecrated (prāṇa-pratiṣṭhā) on 22 January 2024; many Hindus regard the site as Rāma’s birthplace (Rāma Janmabhūmi).
details: The site was previously occupied by the Babri Masjid, a mosque built around 1528–29 under the Mughal emperor Babur and demolished in 1992. In its 2019 judgment the Supreme Court awarded the disputed land for the construction of a temple by a trust and directed that alternative land be allotted for a mosque (at Dhannipur). Construction under the Shri Ram Janmbhoomi Teerth Kshetra trust began after a bhūmi-pūjana in August 2020. The principal image consecrated in 2024 is the child Rāma (Bālak Rām); the earlier Rām Lallā Virājmān image of 1949 is also kept in the sanctum.

dates.label: Site regarded by many Hindus as Rāma’s birthplace (tradition)
dates.basis: temple tradition (sthala-purāṇa / local narrative); not a historical date

limits: A 21st-century building; it documents contemporary religious practice. The identification of the site as Rāma’s birthplace is a matter of faith, which the Supreme Court judgment did not decide as historical fact.

name: Kedāranātha temple
summary: High-altitude stone temple of Śiva at about 3,580 m in the Garhwal Himalaya, a jyotirliṅga, one of the Chota Char Dham and the chief of the Pañca Kedāra; it survived the 2013 flash flood that devastated the town.
details: Legend credits the Pāṇḍavas with the first temple and associates Ādi Śaṅkara with its revival and with his death nearby; neither is documented. Who built the present temple, and when, is not certain. The liṅga is an irregular rock worshipped as the hump of Śiva in bull form. The temple is open only from about May to November.

dates.label: First temple built by the Pāṇḍavas seeking Śiva’s forgiveness after the war (tradition)
dates.basis: temple tradition (sthala-purāṇa / local narrative); not a historical date

name: Badrīnātha temple
summary: Temple of Viṣṇu as Badrīnārāyaṇa at about 3,100 m on the Alaknandā, the northern dhāma of the Char Dham, one of the Chota Char Dham and a Divya Deśam; it was largely rebuilt after the 1803 Garhwal earthquake.
details: Tradition holds that Ādi Śaṅkara recovered the image from the Alaknandā and re-established worship; the chief priest (Rāval) is still a Nambūdiri brāhmaṇa from Kerala. After the earthquake of 1803 the temple was largely rebuilt with support from the King of Jaipur. It is administered with Kedarnath by the Shri Badarinath–Kedarnath Temple Committee.

name: Gaṅgotrī temple
summary: Temple of the goddess Gaṅgā at about 3,100 m on the Bhāgīrathī, one of the Chota Char Dham; the original temple was built in the early 19th century by the Gorkha general Amar Singh Thapa.
details: Tradition places here the penance of King Bhagīratha that brought the Gaṅgā down from heaven. The glacier source at Gaumukh lies about 18 km upstream.

dates.label: Bhagīratha’s penance brought the Gaṅgā to earth here (tradition)
dates.basis: temple tradition (sthala-purāṇa / local narrative); not a historical date

limits: The temple is 19th century; coordinates are those of Gangotri town.

name: Yamunotrī temple
summary: Temple of the river goddess Yamunā near the source of the Yamunā in the Garhwal Himalaya, the westernmost of the Chota Char Dham; built in the 19th century by a ruler of Tehri Garhwal and rebuilt after destruction by snow and floods.
details: Pilgrims cook rice in the hot spring Sūrya Kuṇḍa as an offering.

dates.label: 19th c. CE (Mahārāja Pratāp Śāh of Tehri Garhwal per Wikipedia), rebuilt since

limits: Coordinates are approximate.

name: Jageśvara temple group
summary: Group of more than 100 stone temples (7th–14th c.) in a deodar valley near Almora, claimed locally as the Nāgeśa jyotirliṅga “in the Dāruka forest”; ASI-protected.
details: Over 200 structural temples are spread over the valley clusters. Wikipedia notes that the tradition crediting Ādi Śaṅkara has no textual or epigraphic support, and that the temples were patronised and maintained by Pāśupata ascetics (including a Lakulīśa temple).
limits: The jyotirliṅga claim competes with Dwarka and Aundha.

name: Mārtaṇḍa Sun temple, Kashmir
summary: Ruined 8th-century temple of Sūrya (Mārtaṇḍa) on a plateau near Anantnag, built by the Kārkoṭa king Lalitāditya Muktāpīḍa according to Kalhaṇa’s Rājataraṅgiṇī and destroyed in the early 15th century.
details: The temple stood in a colonnaded courtyard with a trefoil-arched peristyle characteristic of Kashmiri architecture. Kalhaṇa (12th c.) credits Lalitāditya with the temple. Later chroniclers (Jonarāja) attribute its destruction to Sultan Sikandar (r. 1389–1413). The ruins are ASI-protected.

location.label: Mattan, Anantnag district, Jammu and Kashmir, India

image.credit: Varun Shiv Kapur from New Delhi, India (Wikimedia Commons)

limits: The patron is known from a 12th-century chronicle written four centuries later; the ruin shows Saura royal worship in 8th-c. Kashmir.

name: Paśupatinātha temple, Kathmandu
summary: Pagoda-roofed temple of Śiva as Paśupati (“Lord of creatures”) on the Bāgmatī at Deopatan, Kathmandu, Nepal’s principal Hindu shrine; worship here is attested from the Licchavi period, and the present building dates from a renovation of 1692.
details: Chronicles such as the Gopālarājavaṃśāvalī attribute an early temple to the Licchavi king Pracaṇḍadeva; Licchavi inscriptions from the 5th–8th centuries in the area attest the cult of Paśupati. The present two-tiered pagoda was renovated in 1692 after damage by termites and earthquakes (Wikipedia, citing Sharma). Cremation ghāṭs line the river, and the Guhyeśvarī temple nearby is counted as a Śakti Pīṭha. The temple’s priests (Bhaṭṭas) have long been brāhmaṇas from South India. Part of the Kathmandu Valley World Heritage property.

dates.label: Śiva as a deer in the Śleṣmāntaka forest; liṅga revealed by a cow (Nepāla-māhātmya tradition)
dates.basis: temple tradition (sthala-purāṇa / local narrative); not a historical date

dates.label: cult attested from the Licchavi period (5th–8th c. inscriptions)
1692 CE renovation (present form)
dates.basis: secondary account (Sharma, via Wikipedia); other sources give 1697

attributes.unesco: Kathmandu Valley — inscribed 1979; UNESCO list no. 121 (Pashupati component, 121bis-006 per Wikipedia)

limits: The building is late 17th century; Licchavi inscriptions attest the cult of Paśupati but not the present structure.

name: Changu Narayan temple
summary: Hilltop Viṣṇu temple east of Kathmandu that preserves the pillar inscription of the Licchavi king Mānadeva (Saṃvat 386, 464 CE), the earliest dated inscription of Nepal; the two-tiered pagoda itself is a later rebuilding, heavily damaged in 2015 and restored.
details: The site holds outstanding Licchavi sculptures of Viṣṇu (Viśvarūpa, Trivikrama, Garuḍa). The present pagoda was rebuilt after a fire around 1702 (recall; not verified online) and reconstructed with Chinese assistance after the 2015 earthquake. Part of the Kathmandu Valley World Heritage property.

attributes.unesco: Kathmandu Valley — inscribed 1979; UNESCO list no. 121 (Changu Narayan component, 121bis-007 per Wikipedia)

image.credit: Dhilung Kirat from Santa Barbara, CA (Wikimedia Commons)

limits: The inscription and Licchavi sculptures establish 5th-c. Vaiṣṇava royal worship at the site; the standing pagoda is early modern.

name: Jānakī Mandir, Janakpur
summary: White marble-and-stone temple of Sītā (Jānakī) at Janakpur, Nepal, built in 1910 by Queen Vṛṣabhānu of Tikamgarh (Orchha) in a Hindu–Rajput (Mughal-influenced) style; Janakpur is identified by tradition with Mithilā, Sītā’s city.
details: The temple is a focus of the Vivāha Pañcamī festival celebrating the marriage of Rāma and Sītā. The surrounding area is a protected monument zone under Nepal’s Ancient Monuments Preservation Act, 1956.

dates.label: Janakpur is Mithilā, where Sītā was found in a furrow and married Rāma (tradition)
dates.basis: temple tradition (sthala-purāṇa / local narrative); not a historical date

limits: A modern building; the identification of Janakpur with the epic Mithilā is tradition.

name: Muktinātha temple
summary: High-altitude pagoda shrine (c. 3,700 m) in Mustang, Nepal, sacred to Hindus as Viṣṇu Muktinārāyaṇa — a Divya Deśam (Sāḷagrāmam) — and to Tibetan Buddhists as Chumig Gyatsa, an abode of Avalokiteśvara.
details: The temple has 108 water spouts and a nearby spring where natural gas burns over water (Jvālā Māī). The present shrine was built c. 1814–1815, credited to Queen Subarna Prabha Devi of Nepal. The Gaṇḍakī valley below is the source of the śālagrāma fossil stones used in Viṣṇu worship.

location.label: Ranipauwa, Mustang District, Gandaki Province, Nepal

limits: Shared Hindu and Buddhist sanctity is documented in practice; the shrine’s fabric is early 19th century.

name: Kōṇēsvaram temple, Trincomalee
summary: Śiva temple on Swami Rock above Trincomalee bay, Sri Lanka, praised in the Tēvāram hymns of Campantar and Cuntarar; the medieval complex was destroyed by the Portuguese in 1622–1624 and a fort built from its stones, and the temple was rebuilt in 1952.
details: The temple is the foremost of the five ancient Īśvarams of Sri Lanka. The Kōṇēcar Kalveṭṭu and Tamil literature describe its patronage; the Polonnaruwa king Gajabāhu II (r. 1131–1153) is remembered as a benefactor. Some lists of the eighteen Mahāśakti Pīṭhas name “Laṅkā (Śāṅkarī)”, which tradition places at Trincomalee — an identification also contested.

dates.label: Ancient shrine linked by tradition to Rāvaṇa’s worship of Śiva (temple tradition)
dates.basis: temple tradition (sthala-purāṇa / local narrative); not a historical date

limits: The present temple is a 20th-century rebuilding; early dates claimed in the infobox (6th c. BCE) rest on tradition. The Rāvaṇa association is tradition, and the epic Laṅkā is not assumed to be Sri Lanka.

name: Muṉṉēsvaram temple, Chilaw
summary: Śiva temple near Chilaw on Sri Lanka’s west coast, in existence since at least c. 1000 CE; tradition holds that Rāma worshipped Śiva here after the war with Rāvaṇa. It was destroyed twice by the Portuguese and rebuilt in 1753.
details: The complex includes a Kālī shrine popular with both Hindus and Buddhists. The Kandyan king Kīrti Śrī Rājasiṃha is credited with supporting the 1753 rebuilding (recall).

dates.label: Rāma worshipped Śiva here after killing Rāvaṇa (tradition)
dates.basis: temple tradition (sthala-purāṇa / local narrative); not a historical date

dates.label: in existence at least since c. 1000 CE (probable)

location.label: Munneswaram, Chilaw, North Western Province, Sri Lanka

limits: The Rāma association is tradition; the present fabric is post-1753.

name: Katās Rāj temples
summary: Group of Hindu temples (6th century onward) around a sacred pond in the Salt Range of Punjab, Pakistan; tradition holds that the pond formed from Śiva’s tears after Satī’s death and that the Pāṇḍavas met the Yakṣa here.
details: The name is derived from Sanskrit kaṭākṣa (“tearful eyes”). Indian pilgrims visited for Mahāśivarātri until 1965 and again from 1984. Pakistan began a restoration project in 2006.

dates.label: Pond formed from Śiva’s tears for Satī; Yakṣa-praśna of the Pāṇḍavas (tradition)
dates.basis: temple tradition (sthala-purāṇa / local narrative); not a historical date

dates.label: 6th c. CE onward (most temples later, c. 10th c.)

limits: Dating of individual temples was not verified; associations with Satī and the Mahābhārata are tradition.

name: Hiṅglāj Mātā cave shrine
summary: Natural cave shrine of the goddess Hiṅgulā in the Hingol valley of Balochistan, Pakistan, counted as a Śakti Pīṭha where part of Satī’s head fell; the spring Hinglaj Yātrā draws very large numbers of pilgrims and is also revered by local Muslims as “Nani”.
details: The Hinglaj Sheva Mandali, founded in 1986, organises pilgrim services; a wall built by it in 1996 marks the entrance to the valley. The shrine is a natural cave with modern facilities rather than an architectural temple.

dates.label: Part of Satī’s head fell here (pīṭha tradition)
dates.basis: temple tradition (sthala-purāṇa / local narrative); not a historical date

location.label: Hingol National Park, Lasbela District, Balochistan, Pakistan

limits: No historic architecture is dated here; the pīṭha identity is tradition. Coordinates are approximate.

name: Prambanan (Candi Rara Jonggrang)
summary: Ninth-century Hindu temple compound in Central Java with towering shrines to Śiva, Brahmā and Viṣṇu; it is identified with the Śiva temple whose inauguration on 12 November 856 is recorded in the Śivagṛha inscription, and its balustrade reliefs tell the Rāmāyaṇa and the Kṛṣṇa story.
details: Construction was probably begun by Rakai Pikatan of Medang (a painted name “pikatan” was found on a finial of the Śiva temple) and inaugurated by his successor Lokapāla. The Śivagṛha inscription (856), edited by de Casparis, describes a Śiva temple compound and a river diversion that closely match Prambanan. The Rāmāyaṇa reliefs run on the Śiva and Brahmā temples, the Kṛṣṇāyana on the Viṣṇu temple. Prambanan Temple Compounds were inscribed as a World Heritage property in 1991.

dates.label: Legend of Rara Jonggrang, the princess turned to stone (Javanese folk tradition)
dates.basis: temple tradition (sthala-purāṇa / local narrative); not a historical date

dates.label: 12 November 856 CE (Śivagṛha inscription)
dates.basis: dated inscription identified with the compound

dates.label: c. 850 CE (begun under Rakai Pikatan)
dates.basis: painted name on finial and inscription

location.label: Prambanan, Sleman Regency, Yogyakarta / Central Java, Indonesia

attributes.unesco: Prambanan Temple Compounds — inscribed 1991; UNESCO list no. 642

limits: The identification of the Śivagṛha inscription with Prambanan is a strong scholarly argument (class 5), not an inscription found on the temple. The reliefs show a Javanese Rāmāyaṇa tradition, not the events themselves.

name: Arjuna temple group, Dieng Plateau
summary: Small Śaiva stone temples on the volcanic Dieng Plateau of Central Java (mid-7th to late 8th c.), among the oldest standing stone structures in Java; their Mahābhārata names (Arjuna, Semar, Srikandi, Puntadewa) were given much later by local people.
details: Dates for the Dieng temples range from the mid-7th to the end of the 8th century; an inscription of 809 CE is often cited for the site (not verified here).

location.label: Dieng Plateau, Banjarnegara Regency, Central Java, Indonesia

limits: The Pāṇḍava names are modern and do not indicate original dedications or any link with the Mahābhārata.

name: Angkor Wat
summary: State temple of the Khmer king Sūryavarman II (r. 1113–c. 1150), built as a temple-mountain to Viṣṇu at Yaśodharapura (Angkor); its galleries carry vast bas-reliefs of the churning of the ocean, the Kurukṣetra battle and the war in Laṅkā. From the late 13th century it became a Theravāda Buddhist monastery.
details: The temple faces west, unusually, which has been linked to Viṣṇu and to a funerary function. The western gallery shows the Battle of Laṅkā (northern half) and the Kurukṣetra war (southern half); the eastern gallery shows the Churning of the Ocean of Milk (Samudra-manthana), with 92 asuras and 88 devas pulling the serpent Vāsuki; the northern gallery shows Kṛṣṇa’s victory over Bāṇa; another gallery shows Sūryavarman II himself in procession. Angkor was inscribed as a World Heritage property in 1992. Astronomical alignments proposed by Stencel et al. (1976) and Mannikka (1996) remain debated.

dates.label: c. 1113–1150 CE (reign of Sūryavarman II)
dates.basis: regnal synchronism; labelled relief of the king

dates.label: conversion to Theravāda Buddhist use from the late 13th c.

attributes.unesco: Angkor — inscribed 1992; UNESCO list no. 668
