limits: The reliefs are a 12th-century Khmer reading of Sanskrit epic and Purāṇic narratives; they attest the reception of those texts, not the historicity of the events.

name: Banteay Srei
summary: Small, exquisitely carved red-sandstone Śiva temple near Angkor consecrated on 22 April 967 CE, unusual in having been built not by a king but by the court official Yajñavarāha; its pediments include Rāvaṇa shaking Mount Kailāsa.
details: Yajñavarāha (and Viṣṇukumāra) served as counsellors to Rājendravarman II and tutor to Jayavarman V. The temple’s Khmer name means “citadel of women”, a modern name; its original name was Tribhuvanamaheśvara. Part of the Angkor World Heritage property.

location.label: near Angkor, Siem Reap Province, Cambodia

attributes.unesco: part of Angkor (1992; no. 668)

limits: Securely dated; the Rāvaṇa pediment attests the Rāvaṇānugraha narrative in 10th-c. Cambodia.

name: Preah Vihear temple
summary: Khmer Śiva temple stretched along a north–south axis on a cliff of the Dângrêk escarpment, built mainly in the 11th–12th centuries under Sūryavarman I and Sūryavarman II; the International Court of Justice ruled in 1962 that it lies in Cambodia, and it was inscribed as a World Heritage property in 2008.
details: The temple was dedicated to Śiva as Śikhareśvara (“Lord of the peak”). The 2008 inscription was followed by armed clashes on the border; the ICJ’s 2013 interpretation judgment concerned the surrounding promontory.

location.label: Choam Khsant District, Preah Vihear Province, Cambodia

attributes.unesco: Temple of Preah Vihear — inscribed 2008; UNESCO list no. 1224

limits: The UNESCO list number (1224) is from recall and should be checked on whc.unesco.org (blocked to automated fetching in this session).

name: Vat Phou
summary: Khmer-period Śiva sanctuary at the foot of Mount Phou Kao (Liṅgaparvata, named for its liṅga-shaped summit) in southern Laos, with structures from the 5th to the 13th century; now a Theravāda Buddhist site and a World Heritage property (2001).
details: The sanctuary was associated with the early city of Śreṣṭhapura on the Mekong. Most standing buildings date from the 11th–12th centuries. The World Heritage property is the Vat Phou and Associated Ancient Settlements within the Champasak Cultural Landscape.

attributes.unesco: Vat Phou and Associated Ancient Settlements within the Champasak Cultural Landscape — inscribed 2001; UNESCO list no. 481

limits: UNESCO number (481) from recall. The liṅga-mountain is a natural feature venerated as Śiva.

name: Mỹ Sơn sanctuary
summary: Valley of Cham brick temple-towers in central Vietnam, the principal religious centre of the kings of Champa from the 4th to the 13th century, dedicated chiefly to Śiva as Bhadreśvara; inscribed as a World Heritage property in 1999.
details: The first sanctuary is associated with the 4th-century king Bhadravarman. Many towers were destroyed by US bombing in a single week during the Vietnam War. The valley lies in former Quảng Nam province, which was merged into Đà Nẵng city in Vietnam’s 2025 administrative reorganisation.

location.label: Thu Bồn commune, Đà Nẵng (formerly Quảng Nam province), Vietnam

attributes.unesco: My Son Sanctuary — inscribed 1999; UNESCO list no. 949

limits: UNESCO number (949) from recall; coordinates are for the valley at minute precision.

name: Pura Besakih
summary: The “mother temple” of Balinese Hinduism, a complex of more than twenty temples terraced on the slopes of Mount Agung; in use as a Hindu sanctuary at least since the 14th century.
details: The principal Pura Penataran Agung is dedicated to Śiva, with associated temples for Brahmā and Viṣṇu. Wikipedia states it was used as a Hindu place of worship from 1284. The complex survived the 1963 eruption of Mount Agung.

dates.label: in Hindu use from the late 13th–14th c. CE

limits: The terraced sanctuary may be older; the buildings themselves are frequently renewed.

name: Batu Caves temple
summary: Murukaṉ shrine in limestone caves north of Kuala Lumpur, completed in 1891 and the focus since 1892 of one of the largest Thaipūsam festivals outside India; a very tall gilded statue of Murukaṉ was unveiled beside the steps in January 2006.
details: The Tamil trader K. Thamboosamy Pillai promoted the caves as a place of Hindu worship, reportedly inspired by the resemblance of the cave mouth to Murukaṉ’s vel (spear). Its festival reflects the Tamil diaspora in Malaysia.
limits: A diaspora foundation of the colonial period; it shows the reach of Murukaṉ worship, not an ancient sanctuary.

name: Naṭarāja (Śiva as lord of dance)
summary: Śiva as the king of dancers, above all in the South Indian ānanda-tāṇḍava form standardised in Cōḻa bronzes: four-armed, dancing within a ring of flames on the dwarf Apasmāra, worshipped above all at Chidambaram.
details:
Dancing forms of Śiva appear in Deccan cave sculpture from the 6th century (e.g. the many-armed dancer of Bādāmi Cave 1 and the Elephanta panel). The canonical Tamil ānanda-tāṇḍava type, with the drum (ḍamaru), fire, the abhaya gesture and the raised leg, was fixed in bronze under the Cōḻas by the 10th century. Śaiva Siddhānta theology reads the dance as Śiva’s five acts (pañcakṛtya): creation, preservation, destruction, concealment and grace.

In the Chidambaram tradition Naṭarāja dances in the golden hall before the sages Patañjali and Vyāghrapāda. The form is a Tamil and wider South Asian theological elaboration of Śiva; this dataset treats it as FORM_OF Śiva, qualified by tradition, not as a separate god.

dates.label: 6th c. CE (Deccan cave temples)
dates.basis: dated and stylistically dated cave reliefs (Bādāmi Cave 1, Elephanta)

dates.label: by the 10th c. CE (Cōḻa bronzes)
dates.basis: dated bronzes and inscriptions recording gifts of images

limits: Images and texts establish the history of the iconographic form and its theology; they say nothing about the antiquity of the idea of Śiva’s dance beyond the dated evidence.

name: Jagannātha
summary: “Lord of the world”, the deity of Puri worshipped in a stylised wooden image with large round eyes and stump arms, together with Balabhadra and Subhadrā; Vaiṣṇavas regard him as Viṣṇu/Kṛṣṇa, while scholars debate the cult’s tribal, Vaiṣṇava, Buddhist and Jain antecedents.
details:
The images are renewed in the Navakalevara rite (most recently 1996 and 2015), when the “life substance” is transferred to new figures carved from specially chosen nīm trees, and the Daitā priests — said to descend from the Śabara chief Viśvāvasu of the temple legend — have a central role. The Indradyumna legend itself tells that the deity was first worshipped by a Śabara as Nīlamādhava.

Eschmann, Kulke and Tripathi (1978) argued that Jagannātha developed from a tribal wooden deity progressively “Hinduised” and made into an imperial Vaiṣṇava cult by the Eastern Gaṅga kings, who styled themselves the god’s deputies; nineteenth-century writers proposed Buddhist origins (relic, triratna), which most modern scholars reject. For the Gauḍīya tradition, Caitanya’s ecstatic devotion at Puri identified Jagannātha with Kṛṣṇa.
limits: The temple, rituals and inscriptions document the cult from the 12th century; its earlier origins are reconstructed and contested.
openQuestions: Which pre-12th-century references to Puruṣottama/Puri refer to the same cult?

name: The tribal (Śabara) origin hypothesis for Jagannātha
summary: The scholarly hypothesis that Jagannātha began as a wooden deity of tribal (Śabara) communities of Odisha and was progressively integrated into Brahmanical Vaiṣṇavism and royal cult, culminating under the Eastern Gaṅgas.
details: Argued in Eschmann, Kulke and Tripathi (eds.) 1978. Supporting points: the aniconic wooden images and their periodic renewal, the role of the Daitā (non-brāhmaṇa) servitors, and the temple’s own Śabara legend. Competing views: Buddhist-origin theories of the 19th century; a continuous Vaiṣṇava (Puruṣottama) cult; Jain readings. The claim concerns history, not the theology of the tradition, which regards Jagannātha as Viṣṇu/Kṛṣṇa.

name: The claim that the Muṇḍeśvarī temple dates to 108 CE
summary: The claim, displayed by the ASI and the Bihar State Religious Trust Board, that the Muṇḍeśvarī temple was built in 108 CE and is the oldest functioning Hindu temple in the world.
details: The claim reads the year 30 of an inscription of Mahārāja Udayasena as Śaka 30. Palaeography indicates a post-Gupta script (Neuss: c. 570–590 CE), and a Harṣa-era reading gives 636 CE; architectural historians date the surviving sculpture to the 6th–7th century and have suggested that the octagonal shrine itself is a later reconstruction.

name: Veṅkaṭeśvara
summary: Viṣṇu as Lord of the Vēṅkaṭa hill, worshipped at Tirumala in a standing four-armed image; one of the most widely worshipped forms of Viṣṇu in South India and the diaspora.
details: The hill is praised by the Āḻvārs, and the temple’s epigraphy runs from the 10th century. The Veṅkaṭācala-māhātmya tells how Viṣṇu came to the hill as Śrīnivāsa and married Padmāvatī, borrowing from Kubera for the wedding — a debt devotees help repay through offerings. Older sectarian polemics debated whether the image was originally Vaiṣṇava, Śaiva, Śākta or Murukaṉ; the Śrīvaiṣṇava tradition credits Rāmānuja with settling its Vaiṣṇava identity.
limits: Hymns and inscriptions date the cult’s history; the descent narrative is the tradition’s own.

name: Mīnākṣī
summary: The “fish-eyed” goddess of Madurai, who in the temple’s myth is born as a three-breasted Pāṇḍya princess, conquers the world and marries Śiva as Sundareśvara; she is identified with Pārvatī.
details: The myth is told in the Tiruviḷaiyāṭaṟpurāṇam and enacted at the Cittirai festival. Fuller (1984) documents the priests and ritual of her temple.
limits: A regional goddess integrated into Śaiva theology; the Pāṇḍya-princess story is temple mythology.

name: Raṅganātha
summary: Viṣṇu reclining on the serpent Ādiśeṣa, “lord of the stage (raṅga)”, worshipped above all at Srirangam on the Kāvēri.
limits: A temple-specific form; theological identity with Viṣṇu is recorded as FORM_OF.

name: Yamunā
summary: The river Yamunā personified as a goddess, daughter of Sūrya and sister of Yama, worshipped at her Himalayan source at Yamunotri and along the river, notably at Mathurā and Vṛndāvana.
limits: Thin record created to anchor the Yamunotri temple.

name: Hampi
summary: Ruined capital of the Vijayanagara empire on the Tuṅgabhadrā in Karnataka, a pilgrimage centre of Virūpākṣa–Pampā and, in local tradition, the Kiṣkindhā of the Rāmāyaṇa; the Group of Monuments at Hampi was inscribed on the World Heritage List in 1986.
details: The city flourished from the mid-14th century until it was sacked in 1565 after the battle of Tāḷikōṭa. Local tradition identifies its rocky landscape with Kiṣkindhā, the monkey kingdom: Ṛṣyamūka, Mataṅga hill and the Añjanādri hill (claimed as Hanumān’s birthplace, a claim also made for Añjanerī near Nashik and Tirumala’s Añjanādri) lie around the river. The World Heritage property was on the List in Danger from 1999 to 2006.

attributes.unesco: Group of Monuments at Hampi — inscribed 1986; UNESCO list no. 241 (List in Danger 1999–2006)

limits: Archaeology documents the Vijayanagara city and its temples; the identification with Kiṣkindhā is tradition and does not locate the epic geography.

name: Adam’s Bridge (Rāma Setu)
summary: Chain of limestone shoals and sandbanks, about 48 km long, between Pamban (Rameswaram) Island in India and Mannar Island in Sri Lanka; Hindu tradition identifies it with the causeway built by Rāma’s army to reach Laṅkā.
details: Geologists regard the shoals as a natural formation of sand and coral-derived limestone shaped by sea-level change and longshore currents; claims that it is a man-made structure are treated separately (claim:rama-setu-built). The name “Adam’s Bridge” derives from Islamic tradition. The identification with Rāma’s setu is ancient in the pilgrimage tradition of Rameswaram–Dhanushkodi, but the critical text of the Rāmāyaṇa does not locate the setu by modern geography, and this dataset keeps the epic’s Laṅkā distinct from Sri Lanka.

location.label: Palk Strait between Pamban Island (India) and Mannar Island (Sri Lanka)

limits: The physical feature is natural by current geological consensus; its sanctity is a matter of tradition and says nothing about the historicity of the setu-bandha episode.

name: Rameswaram (Pamban island)
summary: Island in the Gulf of Mannar off Tamil Nadu, linked to the mainland by the Pamban bridges, home of the Rāmanāthasvāmī temple and of Dhanushkodi at its south-eastern tip, where pilgrimage tradition places the start of Rāma’s bridge.
details: Dhanushkodi was destroyed by the 1964 cyclone. The island’s pilgrimage circuit includes bathing at Agnitīrtham and the 22 wells in the temple.
limits: Island geography and pilgrimage practice; the Rāmāyaṇa associations are tradition.

name: Rājarāja I
summary: Cōḻa king (r. 985–1014) whose conquests made the Cōḻas the leading power of South India; builder of the Bṛhadīśvara temple at Thanjavur.
limits: Regnal dates are approximate and follow standard chronologies; this record exists to anchor temple patronage.

name: Rājendra I
summary: Cōḻa king (r. 1014–1044), son of Rājarāja I, whose northern expedition reached the Gaṅgā and whose navy raided Śrīvijaya; founder of Gaṅgaikoṇḍacōḻapuram.
limits: Regnal dates are approximate and follow standard chronologies; this record exists to anchor temple patronage.

name: Rājarāja II
summary: Later Cōḻa king (r. c. 1146–1173) under whom the Airāvateśvara temple at Darasuram was built.
limits: Regnal dates are approximate and follow standard chronologies; this record exists to anchor temple patronage.

name: Parāntaka I
summary: Early Cōḻa king (r. c. 907–955) credited in copper-plate inscriptions with covering the roof of Naṭarāja’s hall at Chidambaram with gold.

name: Divya Deśams (the 108)
summary: The 108 abodes of Viṣṇu sung by the twelve Āḻvār poet-saints in the Nālāyira Divya Prabandham; 105 are in India, one in Nepal (Muktinath/Sāḷagrāmam), and two (Tiruppāṟkaṭal, the milk ocean, and Paramapadam) are beyond the earth.
details: The list is central to Śrīvaiṣṇava pilgrimage and theology. Srirangam is counted first. Most are in Tamil Nadu and Kerala; northern members include Badrinath, Ayodhyā, Naimiṣāraṇya, Mathurā and Dvārakā.
limits: A network is a traditional list; membership claims are religious tradition (class 6) and lists differ by text and region. Inclusion in a list does not date a temple.

name: Pāṭal Peṟṟa Talaṅkaḷ (the 276 Tēvāram shrines)
summary: The 276 Śiva temples praised in the Tēvāram hymns of the three Nāyaṉmār Appar, Campantar (Sambandar) and Cuntarar (Sundarar), 7th–9th c.; most are in the Kāvēri delta, with a few in Sri Lanka, northern India and the Himalaya.
details: Being “sung” in the Tēvāram is a defining mark of antiquity and sanctity in Tamil Śaiva tradition. The Sri Lankan members are Kōṇēsvaram (Trincomalee) and Kētīsvaram (Mannar); northern members include Kedarnath and Mount Kailāsa. Temples founded after the hymns (such as Thanjavur’s Bṛhadīśvara) are not on the list.
limits: A network is a traditional list; membership claims are religious tradition (class 6) and lists differ by text and region. Inclusion in a list does not date a temple.

name: Char Dham (the four dhāmas)
summary: Four pilgrimage “abodes” at the corners of India — Badrinath (north), Dwarka (west), Puri (east) and Rameswaram (south) — associated in tradition with Ādi Śaṅkara.
details: Three are Vaiṣṇava and Rameswaram Śaiva. The scheme is often aligned with the four maṭhas attributed to Śaṅkara (Jyotirmaṭh near Badrinath, Dvārakā, Govardhana at Puri and Śṛṅgeri — the last not at Rameswaram), a link that is traditional. Not to be confused with the Chota Char Dham of Uttarakhand.
limits: A network is a traditional list; membership claims are religious tradition (class 6) and lists differ by text and region. Inclusion in a list does not date a temple.

name: Chota Char Dham (Uttarakhand)
summary: Circuit of four Himalayan shrines in Garhwal — Yamunotri, Gangotri, Kedarnath and Badrinath — that became a mass pilgrimage after road access in the second half of the 20th century.
details: The circuit is traditionally made west to east, from Yamunotri to Badrinath. Seasonal opening runs roughly from April/May to October/November.
limits: A network is a traditional list; membership claims are religious tradition (class 6) and lists differ by text and region. Inclusion in a list does not date a temple.

name: Pañca Bhūta Sthalas (five element liṅgas)
summary: Five South Indian Śiva temples each identified with one of the five elements: earth (Kanchipuram Ekāmbareśvara), water (Tiruvanaikaval Jambukeśvara), fire (Tiruvannamalai Aruṇācaleśvara), air (Srikalahasti) and space/ether (Chidambaram).
details: Four are in Tamil Nadu and one (Srikalahasti) in Andhra Pradesh. Some versions give Tiruvarur rather than Kanchipuram as the earth shrine (recall; not verified).
limits: A network is a traditional list; membership claims are religious tradition (class 6) and lists differ by text and region. Inclusion in a list does not date a temple.

name: Āṟupaṭai Vīṭu (six abodes of Murukaṉ)
summary: Six Tamil Nadu shrines of Murukaṉ — Tirupparankundram, Tiruchendur, Palani, Swamimalai, Tiruttani and Pazhamudircholai — traditionally identified with the places named in Nakkīrar’s Tirumurukāṟṟuppaṭai, a guide-poem of the Pattuppāṭṭu.
details: The poem’s fifth “abode” is a general reference to Murukaṉ dancing on every hill (kuṉṟutōṟāṭal), conventionally assigned to Tiruttani, and the identification of the sixth with the modern Pazhamudircholai shrine is also traditional. Clothey (1978) analyses the network and its history.
limits: A network is a traditional list; membership claims are religious tradition (class 6) and lists differ by text and region. Inclusion in a list does not date a temple.

name: Rival identifications of jyotirliṅga sites
summary: The question of which modern temple corresponds to several of the twelve jyotirliṅgas named in the Śiva Purāṇa list, where the text gives only a region or an ambiguous name: Vaidyanātha, Nāgeśa, Bhīmaśaṅkara and Oṃkāra/Amaleśvara.
details: Vaidyanātha (“at the cremation ground”, citābhūmi): Deoghar (Jharkhand) is most widely accepted; Parli (Maharashtra) and Baijnath (Himachal Pradesh) are rival claimants. Nāgeśa (“in the Dārukā forest”): Nāgeśvara near Dwarka, Aundha Nāganātha (Maharashtra) and Jageshwar (Uttarakhand) all claim it. Bhīmaśaṅkara (“in Ḍākinī”): the Pune-district temple is most visited, but sites in Assam (near Guwahati) and Odisha are also claimed. Oṃkāra: the jyotirliṅga is shared in tradition between Oṃkāreśvara on Māndhātā island and Amaleśvara (Mamaleśvara) on the south bank. These are competing traditions; none can be settled by archaeology, since the list is a textual and devotional construct.
